paragraphs: The following judgments concern massage therapists' service and treatment practices. They do not predict hiring, licensing, qualification, or diagnosis and treatment outcomes, or replace medical assessment.

The core work of massage therapists is to manipulate soft tissues and joints to relieve symptoms and support health: discuss clients' medical histories, stress, and pain; assess soft tissue conditions, joint function, strength, and range of motion; develop and recommend treatment plans as needed; massage and knead muscles and soft tissues and apply pressure to specific areas; guide posture improvement, stretching, and relaxation exercises; maintain treatment records; refer to other therapists or collaborate with physicians, physical therapists, and chiropractors when needed; and clean and disinfect equipment and work areas.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional client service form and health questionnaire, including 1 description of stress, pain, and medical history, 1 set of range-of-motion and strength observation points, and 1 situation requiring referral or modified techniques. Within 60 minutes, write an assessment approach, proposed techniques, contraindication and referral boundaries, and documentation points. Do not use real client or medical data or make diagnoses from it.

Sample output and reflection: check whether medical history and contraindications were established first, observations were distinguished from judgments, referral situations were stated, and hygiene and documentation requirements were explained. Then ask yourself whether you can stand for long periods and repeat manual techniques, control pressure within comfort and safety boundaries, and willingly continue practice under licensing and hygiene standards.

This page corresponds to US ONet31-9011.00, primarily soft tissue / joint massage, potentially assisting with range-of-motion / strength assessment and service planning. Medical-history discussions, techniques, hygiene, records, and referrals remain within competence and state authority and do not replace chiropractic, physical / occupational, or radiation therapy. Chinese wellness services cannot copy US treatment responsibilities: the 2023 traditional Chinese medicine health maintenance standards apply to corresponding nonmedical institutions, prohibiting diagnosis and treatment, hazardous methods such as traction / manipulation, or treatment claims. Medical-institution tasks follow separate competent authority rules.

entries: Inputs: client medical history, stress, and pain information, health questionnaires and informed consent, soft tissue and joint conditions, range-of-motion and strength observations, manual techniques and auxiliary supplies, treatment records and referral information, and hygiene and practice standards.

Checkable outputs: assessment and technique-choice explanations, treatment plans, treatment processes and records, posture and relaxation exercise guidance, referral and consultation records, hygiene and disinfection records, and service environment and equipment conditions.

Complete workflow: review medical history and confirm informed consent → assess soft tissue and joint conditions → develop and recommend treatment plans → provide manual treatment → guide exercises and self-care → document and judge referral needs → clean, disinfect, and organize.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether clients have massage contraindications or conditions requiring referral, whether technique pressure and scope are safe, whether communication and informed consent are adequate, whether hygiene and disinfection meet standards, and whether services remain within licensing and competence.

Environment and pace: primarily controlled indoor settings, close physical proximity, continuous hand use and prolonged standing, with many repetitive movements. Most work fewer than 40 hours, with relatively regular schedules; some are self-employed and schedule by client appointments.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 31-9011.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research conclusions do not establish mainland China's qualification, licensing, wage, or employment scope.

Check first: practice licensing or certification requirements, client medical history and contraindications, informed consent and privacy, safe use of techniques and supplies, hygiene and disinfection standards, and referral situations.

End-to-end work: review medical history and confirm informed consent, assess, develop treatment plans, provide manual treatment, guide exercises, document and judge referral needs, and clean and disinfect. Do not treat before contraindications or safety conditions are confirmed. Refer situations beyond competence or licensing scope.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers only massage therapists. Chiropractors handle spinal adjustment and diagnosis; occupational and physical therapists handle functional rehabilitation; radiation therapists provide radiation therapy; recreational therapists provide recreation-based therapy. Professional practice scopes and statutory responsibilities are not interchangeable with this occupation.
Chiropractors emphasize spinal adjustment and diagnosis with corresponding authorization; massage therapists emphasize manual treatment of soft tissues and joints. Practice scopes differ.
Occupational therapists handle daily functioning and occupational rehabilitation; massage therapists provide soft tissue manual treatment. Goals and authorizations differ.

Physical therapists handle movement-function assessment and rehabilitation treatment; massage therapists may assist with range-of-motion and strength assessment but must not assume physical therapy's statutory responsibilities.
Radiation therapists deliver radiation therapy; massage therapists provide soft tissue manual treatment. Service nature and authorization are entirely different.

Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, consider whether you can stand for long periods and continuously repeat manual techniques, discuss medical history and contraindications and build client trust, assess carefully and adjust techniques within safety boundaries, implement hygiene and documentation standards, and recognize referral needs. Tools such as RIASEC can only propose hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience or licensing.

Positive signals: steady techniques, patience and attention to detail, listening and communication, control of pressure and safety boundaries, hygienic practices, and recognizing and referring abnormalities.

Reasons for caution: difficulty standing for long periods or repeating techniques, limited hand or physical capacity, unwillingness to follow hygiene and safety standards strictly, or difficulty communicating contraindications and boundaries with clients.

Trial activity: using entirely fictional client service forms and health questionnaires, rehearse assessment approaches, technique choices, and referral boundaries, and ask someone else to review them against the records.

The O*NET interest code is SRI (Social–Realistic–Investigative), emphasizing helping others, hands-on work, and investigating physical conditions. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications, much less replace licensing.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through actual manual practice, assessment, and client communication experiences.
Type-based tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Entry pathways and capability stages

ONet's new-hire education responses report 48% postsecondary certificate, 19% high school, and 15% associate degree. Postsecondary does not mean after an associate degree; the one to two years for JobZone3 is a group description. BLS programs may take months to years. Most states regulate practice; verify approved programs, examinations / licensing, or registration by state.

United States: postsecondary massage training and practice, with approved programs / examinations and licensing or registration checked separately in regulating states. ONet lists registered apprenticeship title examples but does not guarantee local enrollment or replace licensing. No exact Chinese occupational qualification mapping was established, but nonmedical traditional Chinese medicine health maintenance institutions have clear service / hygiene / personnel training and data security requirements. They may not provide diagnosis and treatment or claim therapeutic effects.

Education, training, certification, and licensing are different statuses. Training or industry certification does not automatically grant practice authorization. Check licensing or certification for independent services and charging fees by US state and local competent authority. Do not practice without authorization.

Entry stage: practice basic techniques, client communication and medical-history review, hygiene and disinfection, and documentation under supervision. Learn contraindications, referral boundaries, and licensing requirements and retain process records.

Evidence to show: use a reviewable service and documentation description covering assessment approaches, technique choices, hygiene steps, and referral boundaries to demonstrate compliant service under supervision.

Next step: check the target employer's service scope and client populations and state or local licensing or certification and hygiene requirements. Validate assessment, manual, and communication skills through real services under supervision.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience and licensing, workers may handle more complex techniques and client relationships, train newcomers or specialize, or move into private practice, organizational management, and teaching.

source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against the original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 31-9011.00 Massage Therapists (Summary): provides occupational identity, the official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 31-9011.00. Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 31-9011.00 Tasks: provides tasks including massaging and kneading soft tissues, applying pressure to specific areas, assessing soft tissues and joints, developing and recommending treatment plans, maintaining records, referral and consultation, and cleaning and disinfection. Task examples do not mean every position performs every task. O*NET 31-9011.00 Work Context: describes primarily controlled indoor work, physical proximity, repetitive movements and prolonged standing, hand use, and other contexts. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 31-9011.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS Display): 2025 BLS OEWS median wages for this occupation. This page does not display percentile wages. O*NET 31-9011.00 National Employment Trends: employment in 2024 and projections for growth and job openings in 2024—2034. Projections are not a hiring guarantee. Industries: 31-9011.00: the main industries on that page for 2024 are Other Services (Except Public Administration) and Health Care and Social Assistance. Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 31-9011.00 Education and Occupational Preparation: Job Zone 3; most positions require a certificate after an associate degree, approximately 48%, and typically one to two years of training. Education distribution does not establish mandatory requirements for every employer. Licenses & Certifications: 31-9011.00: O*NET provides state licensing and national certification lookup entry points. Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements. BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: Massage Therapists: explains that most states regulate massage therapy and require licensing or certification. This describes US state regulation and does not automatically map to other jurisdictions. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. An exposure index is not an adoption rate, job outcome, or hiring probability. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025: provides average annual wages by industry category for urban non-private and private units, including residential services, repairs, and other services. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individually owned businesses and freelancers. FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Massage Therapists: organizes potentially assisted tasks and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussions. An editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.
